newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria bank sale splits uneasy coalition.
newsitem.headline: Austria bank sale splits uneasy coalition.

text.p: The sale of Austria's second biggest bank, Creditanstalt, has jumped out of a privatisation frying pan and into the political fire, causing serious rifts in the coalition government just a year after a snap election.

Political and economic analysts say what should have been a straight privatisation has instead turned into a left-right political battle, exposing the idiosyncratic way Austria has done business since it embraced democracy anew in 1945.
Last week, in the last few nailbiting days of the tender deadline for Creditanstalt, the privatisation took a dramatic turn when Bank Austria, the country's biggest bank, put in its own bid.
On the surface, it may not look a bad idea -- two Austrian banks merging to create a more competitive player to rank in the top 30 banks within the European Union, one economist said.
But the prospect has instead convulsed the uneasy coalition of the dominant Social Democrats (SPOe) of Chancellor Franz Vranitzky and the conservative People's Party (OeVP).

"It's a problem. Bank Austria is considered to be linked to the SPOe and Creditanstalt is considered to belong to circles close to the OeVP," said Franz Hahn, senior economist with Austria's WIFO economic research institute.

If Bank Austria swallows Creditanstalt, bankers to the former Austro-Hungarian imperial family, the conservatives will be seen handing over control of one of its biggest interests to its rivals. Politically, it may weaken the hand of conservative leader, Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel.
OeVP general secretary Maria Rauch-Kallat said her party had been repeatedly told by the Social Democrats and Bank Austria chiefs that they had no intention of making a bid.
"They lied to us...this is not the way to behave in a coalition," she told Austrian radio.
The final decision for the Creditanstalt sale has to be taken by Finance Minister Viktor Klima -- a Social Democrat.

"Klima has been authorised by parliament to take the decision himself. But I guess he will consult his (OeVP) colleagues because it could otherwise lead to an enormous amount of tension and possibly a break-up," Wifo's Hahn said.
Conservative Economics Minister Johann Farnleitner opposes the Bank Austria bid, saying: "We want to see a genuine privatisation, not a communalisation."
Post-1945 relations between the two parties hit rock bottom in October last year when they clashed over ways to cut a big budget deficit, sparking an early general election.
The bank row is the most serious dispute between them since they restored their partnership in February and agreed public spending cuts in a two-year austerity budget.
The ingrained system of patronage in which jobs and homes used to be allocated according to party allegiance, has waned.

"But the case of the two banks is important as it has major policy implications," said Oxford University professor of government Peter Pulzer. "If Bank Austria wins, it would look like the OeVP was handing over banking control to the SPOe."
Last week, OeVP deputies voted with the far right Freedom Party in parliament to reject the Bank Austria bid and call for a full privatisation of Bank Austria and Creditanstalt.
"The OeVP was delivering a message saying 'we are not prepared to be bullied and we can outvote you'," Pulzer said. "It has to do with saving face and satisfying the lower ranks of the (OeVP) party."
The Finance Ministry said on Monday Union Bank of Switzerland had joined a long-standing EA-Generali led consortium to bid for the government's entire 70 percent stake.
Austrian entrepreneur Karl Wlaschek, who sold off his Billa supermarket chain to Germany's Rewe in July for 15 billion schillings ($1.4 billion) also threw his hat in the ring.

Off the record analysts said that, politically, Klima would do well to give much thought to the other bidders, especially the EA-Generali consortium. Better a few schillings less in the coffers, than vault-fulls of political strife, one said.
($1=10.93 Schilling)
